### 5. 9. THE DISCOURSE TO SUBHA (99)

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

There are these five <term>nīvaraṇā</term> <gloss>hindrances</gloss>, young man. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, young man, are the five hindrances. By these five hindrances, the Brahmin <term>Pokkharasāti Opamañño Subhagavaniko</term> <note>a prominent Brahmin teacher of the time</note> is obstructed, closed in, blocked, and enveloped. That he should know, see, or realize a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, surpassing the human state—this is impossible.

There are these five <term>kāmaguṇā</term> <gloss>strands of sensual pleasure</gloss>, young man. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... flavors cognizable by the tongue... touches cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. Bound by these five strands of sensual pleasure, the Brahmin <term>Pokkharasāti Opamañño Subhagavaniko</term> is infatuated, blinded, and obsessed; he consumes them without seeing the danger or knowing the escape. That he should know, see, or realize a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, surpassing the human state—this is impossible.

What do you think, young man? Suppose one were to light a fire dependent on fuel such as grass and wood, and another were to light a fire without any fuel such as grass and wood. Which of these two fires would have flame, color, and radiance?

"If it were possible, Master <term>Gotama</term> <gloss>the Buddha's family name</gloss>, to light a fire without fuel such as grass and wood, that fire would have flame, color, and radiance."

It is impossible, young man, it cannot happen, that one could light a fire without fuel such as grass and wood, except by one with psychic power. <summary>The Buddha explains to the young man Subha that the five hindrances and five strands of sensual pleasure prevent a person from reaching higher spiritual knowledge. He uses the analogy of a fire requiring fuel to illustrate different types of rapture or joy.</summary>
